Umbilical Findings in a Newborn

hernia vs omphalocele vs gastroschisis · skin-covered and reducible: observe · 1.5 cm and age 5 cutoffs · incarcerationIs there skin over it, and how big and how old is it?

Source vignette Pt – 4-hour-old boy, 38 wk, 3.6 kg, mother 18 with no prenatal care, normal vitals; soft, nontender, skin-covered 1.4 cm bulge just below the umbilical stump that enlarges with crying and reduces with gentle pressure · Q – the most appropriate next step for the mass; options spanned observation, abdominal ultrasound, karyotype, immediate surgery and topical silver nitrate

1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Ask first whether skin covers it. A soft bulge under skin that reduces and enlarges with crying is a congenital umbilical hernia: observe; the diagnosis is clinical.
  • Repair a hernia still present at about age 5, and an incarcerated one urgently at any age; one over 1.5 cm is less likely to close. A moist nub after the cord falls off is a granuloma (silver nitrate); urine or stool from the umbilicus is a remnant tract (US, then excision).
  • Bowel with no skin over it goes to surgery after birth: a membrane sac with the cord on it is an omphalocele, which adds a karyotype and echocardiogram; bare bowel beside a normal cord is gastroschisis.

The umbilical ring normally closes after the intestines return from their physiologic herniation into the cord; a hernia is a ring that has not closed yet, so skin covers it. Incarceration is very rare, and small hernias usually close on their own. Elective repair of a very large defect may be offered after age 2; the board answer stays repair at about age 5 for a persistent hernia.

2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingPoints toAction
Bowel outside the abdomen at delivery, with or without a membraneGastroschisis or omphaloceleCover it with a sterile, moist dressing, place a nasogastric tube, start IV fluids and antibiotics and keep the infant warm; then surgery. When the bowel will not fit, a silo covers it and is tightened over several days: a staged silo repair.
A known hernia now firm, tender, discolored or irreducible, with vomitingIncarcerated umbilical herniaUrgent surgical repair at any age.
3Differential
A bulge at the umbilicus
FindingDecides itNext best step
Umbilical herniaSkin-covered, soft, reducible, grows with crying; common in normal newborns, more with Down syndrome, hypothyroidism, Beckwith-Wiedemann and Ehlers-Danlos; most common in African-American infants.Observe; repair at about age 5 if it persists.
OmphaloceleMidline, at the umbilical ring; bowel, often liver, in a membrane sac with the cord inserting on it; other major malformations, trisomy 13 or 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann.Repair after birth; order a karyotype and echocardiogram first.
GastroschisisFull-thickness defect, usually right of a normal cord; bare, swollen bowel with no sac; not linked to chromosomal abnormalities.Immediate surgery. Other anomalies are uncommon, but malrotation or intestinal atresia comes with it in about a quarter of infants.
A moist or draining umbilicus
FindingDecides itNext best step
Umbilical granulomaA soft, moist, pink or red, pedunculated nub that appears after the cord falls off; no urine or stool.Treat with topical silver nitrate.
Patent urachus (urachal fistula)Clear, urine-like fluid from the umbilicus, more with crying, straining or lying prone; a tract to the bladder.Order abdominal US, then surgical excision.
Patent omphalomesenteric duct (vitelline fistula, persistent vitelline duct)Meconium, stool or mucus from the umbilicus; a tract to the ileum.Order abdominal US, then surgical excision.
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Defect over 1.5 cm in a well infantA hernia less likely to closeKeep observing; repair if still present at about age 5.
Wet, red midline mucosa below the umbilicus, with urine drippingBladder exstrophy; an omphalocele sits at the umbilicus and is not wetExamine for separated pubic bones and epispadias.
Cord still attached after 30 daysOrder a CBC: marked neutrophilia, with infections that form no pus.
Single umbilical artery (two-vessel cord)Congenital and chromosomal anomalies, often renalOrder a renal US.

Pause point. Skin over it means observe; bowel without skin means surgery after birth; a moist nub after the cord falls off means silver nitrate; urine or stool from the umbilicus means US for a remnant tract.

Practice
  1. 4-hour-old boy born at 38 weeks to a mother without prenatal care, well-appearing, with a soft, nontender, skin-covered 1.4 cm bulge just below the umbilical stump that enlarges with crying and reduces with gentle pressure → Observation only → Congenital umbilical hernia
  2. 5-year-old girl, well, with a soft, reducible, skin-covered umbilical bulge present since birth that has not decreased in size; defect about 2 cm; no pain or vomiting → Elective surgical repair → Persistent umbilical hernia
  3. 8-month-old boy with a known umbilical hernia that is now firm, tender, discolored and cannot be reduced; he has vomited three times → Urgent surgical repair → Incarcerated umbilical hernia
  4. 12-day-old girl whose cord fell off 4 days ago, now with a 4 mm moist, red, friable, pedunculated nub at the umbilical base with slight serous drainage; afebrile, no surrounding erythema → Topical silver nitrate → Umbilical granuloma
  5. 3-week-old boy with clear, urine-like fluid leaking from the umbilicus that increases when he cries or strains; the skin around the umbilicus is normal → Patent urachus → Ultrasound, then surgical excision
  6. Term newborn with loops of bare, edematous bowel protruding through a defect to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord, with no covering membrane; vital signs stable → Cover the bowel and arrange immediate surgery → Gastroschisis
  7. Term newborn with a 5 cm midline membrane-covered sac containing bowel and liver at the base of the umbilical cord, with the cord inserting on the sac → Karyotype and echocardiogram → Omphalocele
  8. 7-week-old girl born at home without newborn screening, with a reducible skin-covered umbilical hernia, persistent jaundice, a large tongue, poor tone, constipation and a wide posterior fontanelle → Serum TSH and free T4 → Congenital hypothyroidism
Abdominal wall defect at delivery Exposed bowel dries and loses heat and water, so the cover, decompression, fluids and antibiotics in Urgent risks come before surgery. An omphalocele also needs a karyotype and echocardiogram, because it is linked to trisomy 13 and 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann and heart defects. Gastroschisis is usually free of chromosomal and other anomalies outside the gut.
Pearls An umbilical hernia with prolonged jaundice, a large tongue, poor tone, constipation or a large fontanelle is a reason to check TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), because congenital hypothyroidism is the treatable association · Karyotype is for Down features or an omphalocele, never for an isolated hernia in a normal infant · Silver nitrate is the treatment for a granuloma; an umbilical lesion that keeps draining urine or stool is a remnant tract and needs US and excision
Pairs with Congenital Hypothyroidism covers the screen and treatment when a hernia comes with prolonged jaundice or a large tongue. Inherited Tumor Syndromes covers Beckwith-Wiedemann tumor surveillance. Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function covers delayed cord separation. Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia covers the anomaly screen after a structural defect: VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb) anomalies.
How NBME framed it A sleepy 2-month-old at his first visit, with an umbilical hernia, persistent jaundice and cool extremities, needed thyroid function tests, not karyotype, sweat chloride or head or liver CT.
Transferable rule For a newborn umbilical finding, ask first whether skin covers it. Observe a skin-covered, reducible bulge, and repair it if still present at about age 5 or incarcerated at any age. Bowel without skin goes to surgery at birth.
Redundant workupAbdominal ultrasound adds nothing to a clinical diagnosis; it is for an acquired hernia in an older child or adult.
True-fact-wrong-slotImmediate surgery belongs to gastroschisis and omphalocele, where no skin covers the bowel.
Salient decoyA young mother without prenatal care invites a genetic workup, but karyotype is for Down features or an omphalocele, and this infant has neither.
Mirror twinSilver nitrate treats an umbilical granuloma, the moist red nub that appears after the cord falls off, not a skin-covered bulge at 4 hours.
